scene.testo: Sixteen sunrises. Sixteen sunsets. Every single day. You are floating 250 miles above Earth, moving at 17,500 miles per hour, and your alarm just went off. Welcome to the strangest workplace ever built. This is what astronauts actually do all day.

Imagine you are floating inside the International Space Station at 6 AM. Not lying down. Floating. Your sleeping bag is tied to a wall, and your arms drift up in front of you like a sleepwalker's. No up. No down. Just you and a humming machine.

Here is the first surprise. The station runs on Greenwich Mean Time, no matter who you are. The crew lives on one clock, even though the sun rises every 90 minutes outside your window. Your day is a schedule, not a sunrise.

Wake-up time on a typical day is around 6 AM. No coffee pot. No snooze button you can trust. You unzip the bag, grab a handrail, and push off. One tiny kick sends you flying across the module. Nobody walks to the bathroom up here.

Speaking of bathrooms. The toilet uses suction instead of water. You strap your legs down, and a fan pulls everything away. And the water you drink later? NASA has said part of it comes from recycled sweat and urine. Yes, really.

Next, a wash. There is no shower. The crew uses wet towels and rinseless soap, squeezing warm water from a pouch. Water does not fall in space. It clings to your skin in wobbling blobs, so the towel does the work.

Brushing teeth is its own puzzle. You squeeze a little toothpaste, brush, and then you can swallow it or spit into a towel. A drop of water floating loose can drift into the air vents, so every drop is managed.

Now breakfast. Your food comes in pouches, cans, and vacuum-sealed packs. You add hot or cold water through a needle port, then wait. Cereal, scrambled eggs, coffee in a pouch with a straw. Everything is held down with Velcro or tape.

Why the straw and the pouch? Because liquid does not stay in a cup. It forms a floating ball. Crumbs are even worse. A loose crumb can float into your eye or clog a filter. That is why astronauts avoid ordinary bread.

Then comes the daily planning conference. Around 7 AM, the crew talks with mission control on the ground. They review the schedule, check problems, and get the day's task list. The station is a laboratory first, and every minute is planned.

By about 8 AM, the work begins. And here is a number that surprises people. Space station crews often work around 6.5 hours a day on a typical weekday, according to NASA's published schedules. That is a full job, in a place where nothing sits still.

What kind of work? Science. Lots of it. Astronauts run experiments on plants, fluids, flames, human bodies, and materials. On Earth, gravity hides many effects. In orbit, the hidden things float out into view.

Take fire. A candle flame on Earth is teardrop shaped, pulled upward by hot air. In microgravity, NASA experiments have shown flames burn as a small blue sphere. Studying this helps engineers build safer spacecraft.

Then there are plants. Crews have grown lettuce, radishes, and other crops on the station. Astronauts tend them, water them, and measure them. One day, the food for a long trip to Mars may be grown right inside the ship.

Some days are about fixing things. The station is a house that never stops needing repairs. Filters clog. Pumps fail. Air scrubbers need parts. Astronauts act as plumbers, electricians, and mechanics, working with a manual and a call to the ground.

Now the part that surprises everyone. Exercise. Astronauts work out about two hours every day. Not for fun. Without gravity, bones and muscles weaken. NASA has reported that astronauts can lose bone density at roughly 1 percent per month without countermeasures.

They run on a treadmill, strapped in with a harness. They lift using a machine that uses vacuum cylinders to create resistance. They pedal a bike. Sweat does not drip. It sticks to your skin and builds up.

Around midday, lunch. The crew often gathers in one module to eat together. It matters. Spending months in a space the size of a six-bedroom house, with the same few people, makes shared meals a lifeline.

How big is the station really? NASA says its pressurized living space is about the volume of a Boeing 747 jumbo jet. The whole structure stretches roughly 356 feet end to end, about the length of an American football field including end zones.

Afternoons often bring more experiments, maintenance, or a special task. Sometimes a cargo ship arrives. Astronauts use the station's robotic arm to catch it, then spend days unpacking food, science gear, and spare parts.

And sometimes the job takes you outside. A spacewalk. You put on a suit that weighs around 300 pounds on Earth, breathe pure oxygen, and float out through an airlock. Below your boots, the planet slides by at 17,500 mph.

Spacewalks can last six or seven hours. Outside, temperatures swing wildly. NASA says they can range from about minus 250 degrees Fahrenheit in shadow to plus 250 degrees Fahrenheit in direct sunlight. The suit keeps you alive.

One tool slip, and a wrench is gone forever. So everything is tethered. Your safety line clips to the station. Your tools clip to you. Float free, and there is a small jet pack called SAFER built to bring you back.

Back inside, the evening routine begins. Around 6 PM, dinner. Maybe rehydrated pasta, a thermostabilized chicken pouch, or something tortilla-wrapped. Astronauts use tortillas instead of bread, because tortillas barely make crumbs.

After dinner, some free time. Astronauts watch the Earth through the cupola, a window with seven panes. They take photographs. They call family over video. They read, play music, or just float and watch the planet turn.

Many say the view changes them. From orbit, you can see city lights at night, thunderstorms glowing from inside, and the thin blue line of atmosphere. Astronauts have described the atmosphere as shockingly thin, like a coat of paint.

Bedtime is around 9:30 PM station time. You climb into a sleeping bag fixed to a wall, or a small private cabin. You strap yourself in so you do not drift into equipment. Then you close your eyes, and the station hums.

And sleep is tricky. The station orbits Earth about every 90 minutes. That is roughly 16 sunrises a day. Crews cover windows and wear eye masks to fake night. Noise from fans never stops, so earplugs help.

Compare that with your day. You walk to the bathroom. You eat with a fork. You sleep lying down. You shower under falling water. Every single habit you take for granted is rebuilt from scratch in orbit.

And then there is the biggest difference. You cannot leave. A workday on Earth ends when you walk out the door. On the station, the office is your home, your gym, your bedroom, and your lifeboat, for months at a time.

Stays usually last about six months. Some last longer. Over that time, the body changes. Fluids shift toward the head. Faces puff up. Legs get thinner. Astronauts have also reported that their height can increase slightly in space.

Then the day comes to go home. You strap into a Soyuz capsule or a SpaceX Dragon, undock, and fall back toward Earth. Reentry heat outside the capsule climbs to thousands of degrees Fahrenheit. You feel several times your own weight.

And now the strangest part. Back on Earth, gravity feels brutal. Your arm feels like lead. A pen feels heavy. Astronauts have said they instinctively let go of objects, expecting them to float. Some forget, and drop a phone.

So what do astronauts actually do all day? They exercise, repair, experiment, eat from pouches, and watch the world roll by. A job that looks like adventure is really a schedule, with a planet outside the window.

Here is the most surprising detail. Astronauts say the hardest part is not danger. It is routine. And the favorite moment of the day, many say, is the quiet one, floating at a window, watching the sun rise for the sixteenth time.

descrizione:
What do astronauts actually do all day? Follow a real day aboard the International Space Station, from waking up in a sleeping bag at 6 AM to exercising two hours, eating from pouches, running science experiments, and floating through a spacewalk at 17,500 mph.

This documentary uses real NASA footage and documented facts from NASA, ESA, and astronauts' own accounts. You will learn how astronauts eat, sleep, wash, work, and stay healthy 250 miles above Earth, and how their routine compares with yours.

If you love space exploration, life on the ISS, and astronaut daily routines, subscribe to Orbital Days for more stories from orbit.
